extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data collection methods varied across the reviewed datasets, including using NLP algorithms to automatically generate question-answer pairs from existing image captions, and using human annotators to generate questions and answers through both free-form prompting and region-specific prompting.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of images and captions from existing datasets such as NYU-DepthV2, COCO, and YFCC100M, as well as synthetically generated images of shapes.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-human agreement was calculated to assess annotation quality, yielding 83.3% on COCO-VQA, with notably poorer agreement on 'Why' questions.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: An average of 5 human annotations per question for DAQUAR-consensus, and 10 human annotations per question for The VQA Dataset.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm was used to automatically generate question-answer pairs from existing image captions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The datasets exhibit strong language biases, where the phrasing of questions severely constrains the expected answers (e.g., 'yes' is much more common than 'no'). This allows models to exploit regularities in the text rather than genuinely analyzing image content, which impairs the ability to properly evaluate VQA algorithms.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Current VQA datasets are limited by their size, strong biases, and flawed evaluation metrics (such as multiple-choice formats that can be gamed or metrics that reward conflicting ground truth answers). Specific datasets like DAQUAR are too small, restricted to indoor scenes, and feature cluttered images with extreme lighting.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: VQA datasets and systems have the potential to significantly aid blind and visually impaired individuals by allowing them to query and understand visual content in the real world and on the web.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The datasets are used for training, testing, and evaluating Visual Question Answering (VQA) algorithms to assess their ability to perform holistic image understanding and reasoning.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Balancing the dataset by exhaustively pairing every question with every image to eliminate bias.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Using NLP algorithms to derive QA pairs from image captions, which includes breaking longer sentences into smaller chunks for processing.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions. [...] Two distinct modes of data collection were used to make the dataset. In the free-form method, annotators were free to ask any question about an image. [...] prompting workers to ask questions about speciﬁc image regions.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset [39] [...] derives them from the COCO image captions [...] consists of 108,249 images that occur in both YFCC100M [43] and COCO images.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset [39] [...] COCO image captions [...] images that occur in both YFCC100M [43] and COCO images. [...] consists of shapes of varying arrangements, types, and colors.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Using AccuracyV QA, the inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is only 83.3%. [...] Inter-human agreement is especially poor for ‘Why’ questions, with over 59% of these questions having less than three annotators giving exactly the same answer.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: For DAQUAR-consensus, an average of five human annotated ground truth answers per question were collected. [...] For The VQA Dataset, annotators generated ten answers per question.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: In COCO-QA [31], QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Language bias in datasets critically aﬀects the performance of the current VQA systems, which limits their deployment... Dataset bias signiﬁcantly impairs the ability to evaluate VQA algorithms. Questions that require the use of the image content are often relatively easy to answer... In COCO-VQA, ‘yes’ is a much more common answer than ‘no,’ simply because people tend to ask questions biased toward ‘yes’ as an answer.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Existing VQA benchmarks are not suﬃcient to evaluate whether an algorithm has ‘solved’ VQA... Apart from the small size, DAQUAR contains exclusively indoor scenes, which constrains the variety of questions available. The images tend to have signiﬁcant clutter and in some cases extreme lighting conditions

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: The most immediate is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world. For example, as a blind user scrolls through their social media feed, a captioning system can describe the image and then the user could use VQA to query the image to get more insight about the scene.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: These datasets enable VQA systems to be trained and evaluated... An ideal VQA dataset needs to be suﬃciently large to capture the variability within questions, images, and concepts that occur in real world scenarios. It should also have a fair evaluation scheme that is diﬃcult to ‘game’

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: SHAPES consists of 244 unique questions, with every question asked about each of the 64 images in the dataset. Unlike other datasets, this means it is completely balanced and free of bias.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions. [...] Longer sentences are broken into smaller chunks for ease of processing
